title: Fears about toxic lead dust spur battle over US Army plan to detonate bomb-making material in Iowa | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Residents in southeastern Iowa are waiting to learn whether the US Army will detonate five tons of lead azide at a munitions plant after a judge ordered a temporary pause, with environmental activists and local officials expressing concern over possible health risks.

A federal judge ordered the Army topause its plan to detonate the materialat the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in tiny Middletown after environmental groups sued. The detonation, originally scheduled for Friday morning, was moved to Monday.

The Army, in coordination with the US Environmental Protection Agency, plans to destroy nearly 70 drums of lead azide, acompound used to detonatemunitions, the military branch said.

An explosion is meant to destroy material that has become unstable. But the plan has drawn heavy pushback from concerned Iowans, environmental advocates and politicians who worry the plume could spread toxic lead dust – unhealthy at any level and especially dangerous to children – over vast swaths of rural Iowa, the Mississippi River and potentially part of western Illinois.

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds on Friday activated a state emergency operations center, while officials in nearby Illinois are warning residents about dust spilling over into their state.

Here’s what we know about the potential detonation and the legal fight.

The Army inMarchduring “routinestockpile surveillance” discovered lead azide housed in bunkers had been degrading, according to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle. Officials evaluating the best way to dispose of the material communicated with “stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed,” Telle said.

The lead azide’s degraded status left it “extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement,” according to an FAQ distributed by the Army to the community last month. “Packing and transporting it poses an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation to personnel handling and transporting as well as to the public.”

After coordinating with the EPA, experts and the community, officials “determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Telle said.

Army officials held an October 15 community meeting to share information about a potential detonation in late November, according todocuments on the plant’s page. Then, the community this past Sunday got a notice of a detonation on Friday, according to an Armynews release.

After pushback, theArmy rescheduled the detonationto this coming Monday – the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle has said.

Waiting too long to detonate the lead azide could pose more hazards later, he said. Theemergency permitfrom the EPA allows the Army to do the detonation between November 13, 2026, and February 11, 2027.

Still, the problem should have been evaluated 20 years ago, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa professor and environmental health expert.

“Somebody left it to rot that long, for it to now being the only option is to blow it up on site because it can’t be moved,” he told CNN. “It’s regrettable, and it’s almost, it’s hard to believe that it’s happening in this country.”

Officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant have regularly updated officials in Middletown –home to363 people – about the planned detonation, according to Brieanna Beck, the city clerk and municipal officer, who said she has quickly shared each update on the city’s Facebook page. The city has been aware of the detonation plan for about a couple of months, she told CNN in an email.

The Army plant sent letters to homes potentially affected by the detonation, Beck confirmed.

The governor’s office and state agencies were coordinating with EPA and Army officials to “continuously monitor the situation and keep local partners informed,” ReynoldssaidFriday.

But plans and communication around the detonation have gotten strong pushback from environmental advocates, as well as state and federal politicians in Iowa and neighboring Illinois.

Josh Turek, the US senator-elect for Iowa, has called for a delay on the detonation, saying he had “heard from many Iowans who are worried about their health and safety due to the potential risk of lead exposure as a result of the detonation.”

Rob Sand, the incoming governor, said Iowans’ safety now and in the future should be the government’s top concern. “An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation,” hesaid. “The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse.”

Parts of western Illinois, just across the Mississippi River, are included in latestmodeling showing possible exposureto lead dust from the blast. Illinois health and environmental protection officials said they are monitoring the potential detonation and have issued updates to residents.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker on Friday said he spoke with Telle, urging more transparency about the now-paused planned detonation.

“The State is still seeking more data from them on how this could impact Illinoisans and is working to keep you informed and safe,” Pritzkersaid.

Environmental advocates sued the US EPA on Thursday over the emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide, citing concerns about the potential impacts of the explosion.

A federal judge in the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday ordered the Army to pause detonating the lead azide.

The judge’s order didn’t detail when the court would take action on the case, though the EPA in a court filing said it planned to file a response by Sunday, a day before the scheduled detonation.

The Army, in a joint statement with the US Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA, said Friday afternoon, “The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible.”

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement said, adding they will keep local officials and the public updated.

The cleanup requirements under the current permit are inadequate to properly address the scope and degree of potential impacts, according to Thien Chau, a senior attorney at the environmental advocacy nonprofit Earthjustice, who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.

There doesn’t appear to be sufficient understanding of how far the plume would spread, as well as which bodies of water, such as the Mississippi River, and land would be blanketed with lead dust, including where people live, Chau told reporters Friday.

Environmental advocates called on state leaders, including Reynolds, to take control of communication over the potential detonation.

The federal government, including the Army and EPA, couldn’t be trusted to adequately inform Iowans about the risks of the planned detonation, Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, said in a news briefing.

“Iowans deserve a transparent, coordinated, and effective response to this unprecedented event,” Schmidt said.

There is no safe level of lead in the body, Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in astatement. “(And) when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks.”

With the detonation, the hope is if the lead azide spreads over a wider area, it won’t stay in high-level concentrations, according to O’Shaughnessy, the University of Iowa professor.

“It’s kind of like one of these, the solution to pollution is dilution, right?” he said.

There is the potential for exposure through the air during the initial plume or through touch after it has settled, he said, adding neither exposure is worse than the other because the lead will still build up in your body both ways.

However, lead is toxic to the brain. Exposure is known to cause serious harm to children’s health, resulting in slowed growth and development, as well as problems with learning, behavior, hearing and speech, according to theUS Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Environmental advocates also warn of the incident worsening health for residents in Iowa, which has thesecond-highest rate of cancer of any US stateand is only one of three states where the rate is rising.

Thelocal National Weather Service officeforecasts cooler, drier temperatures early next week, with highs in the upper 30s to the mid-40s.

While wind conditions could impact how far lead particles travel, forecast winds blowing from north to south, at around 5 to 10 mph, are also expected, CNN meteorologist Chris Dolce said.

CNN’s Holly Yan, Kara Devlin and Bill Kirkos contributed to this report.

CNN’s Holly Yan, Kara Devlin and Bill Kirkos contributed to this report.
